title: AI agents move factory machinery; contractor malware threatens karaoke records
overview: Booz Allen's lab tests show AI agents reaching industrial controls in minutes, while contractor malware puts millions of karaoke customer records at risk. There are also unfixed WordPress flaws, a published Spug exploit and disputed leaked files from an extortion crew.
paragraphs: Good morning, it's 5:22 AM. Monday, the twelfth of October, twenty twenty-six.

The agent story has crossed onto the factory floor, in a separate lab exercise at Booz Allen Hamilton. Two unnamed frontier models achieved the objectives across all eight OT attack scenarios, without engineering documents or specialist guidance. One found and moved a robotic arm in minutes; another went from perimeter compromise to actions inside the industrial control network in just over sixteen minutes. Human approval was required before exploitation or physical action. That's an important boundary on what these tests demonstrated.

The interesting bit wasn't just speed. When one SCADA attack failed, the agents found editable Jython code in an exported project and rebuilt their payload, taking over an operator screen through the administrative interface. That SCADA gateway already held authenticated sessions to fourteen OT devices, including every PLC they'd encountered. One foothold, rather a lot of machinery. An agent also spotted unanswered ARP requests and proposed claiming the missing address to get a protective relay talking.

I'd take the gateway sessions seriously before getting distracted by which models they used. For manufacturing and critical infrastructure operators, verify the actual firewall paths between enterprise and production zones, and restrict access to engineering interfaces. Audit those pre-authenticated controller sessions; change robot and controller default credentials. Unanswered ARP deserves investigation too. Obscure protocols aren't much of a barrier if an agent can work them out while you're still finding the manual.

And the boundary that matters isn't always inside your own network. Japan's Daiichi Kosho says its systems weren't breached, but malware on a contractor's employee computer put more than eight point seven million customer and employee records at risk. Nippon Columbia reported the discovery on the fifth of October and isolated the machine the following day, then reset credentials. Data theft remains unconfirmed; Friday's update didn't settle that.

The potentially exposed records include contact details and dates of birth for customers of chains including Big Echo, alongside ninety-three thousand employees. Passwords weren't included. Affected customers should be wary of unsolicited requests for payment or personal details. What bugs me is how little reassurance 'our systems weren't breached' buys you here. If you outsource customer-data handling, check what the contractor holds and what notification and investigation your contract actually requires.

From outsourced exposure to code you can remove yourself: seven critical unauthenticated flaws affect six WordPress plugins, with Anton Extensions through 1 point 2 point 2 allowing arbitrary PHP upload and code execution under CVE-2026-104028, scored nine point eight. No fixed releases are named, so deactivate and remove the affected plugins: Anton Extensions, Mindstien Quick Login, Freeton WP, AI Content Generator Marketing, Insurify and Quick quotes; only leave them live with a vendor-confirmed fixed build.

There's another unresolved exposure in OpenSpug Spug, a server-operations console: CVE-2026-108540 allows authenticated command injection through its file-transfer endpoint, slash exec slash transfer, and an exploit is public. Listed affected releases run from 3 point 0 through 4 point 0 point 0; with no vendor response or patch, keep its web interface off the internet and restrict access to that endpoint.

Away from the patch queue, the Luna Moth Files have appeared online: Silent Ransom Group calls them fake and denies a leak, while DataBreaches dot net says they're genuine and leaked rather than being hacked out. That's intelligence on the extortion crew, not a remediation ticket.
I'd remove the exposed, unfixed plugins first where they're in use. For OT teams, I'd check what a compromised SCADA gateway can already reach without another login. Have a good Monday.
